measure.verdict:
Hinge blur does not explain the short attached DNA. On the hinge-insensitive measures the duplex seen on sfGFP is shorter than free duplex for about 88% of dot-at-end particles, which favours H1 (shorter attached duplex) over H2/H3 (full-length, hinge-blurred) for that population. There is also a minority (about 12% of particles, classes 13, 52, 97 and 87) whose attached DNA is as long as free DNA.

My pre-set decision rule returned "mixed/inconclusive", not a clean H1. The only reason is that one class (123) had a weakly positive far-segment angle correlation (r = 0.024, p = 0.002). Even there, the far segment carries only about 0.31 of the angle covariance a rigid full-length rod would give (CI 0.09-0.54), so it fits a small long-DNA minority, not a full-length population.

What rules out hinge blur:
1. Pure rotation about the dot does not move the far end radially. The end of the radial mass profile (density integrated over a ±30° sector) is therefore hinge-insensitive. I checked this by pivoting real free-rod averages: 25° of hinge moves this end by only +1 Å, while the half-max length under-reads by 24 Å.
2. The measured hinge spread is small. In the class averages, the rod width grows with distance as if from an angle of about 6° for dot classes versus 4° for free rods (the difference's 95% CI includes 0). Per particle, the noise-free spread is about 3.2° (0-5.7°). The calibration says that causes at most 4-7 Å of half-max under-read; the observed 33 Å gap would need more than 25°. The reason is geometric: the dot is nearly round at 12 Å, so the 2D in-plane rotation is set by the rod and absorbs an in-plane hinge.
3. Re-aligning the rod body about the dot, with the dot masked, did not lengthen anything. The mass-profile end changed by -1.2 Å (particle-weighted). Mass in the bias-free far zone (100-170 Å from the dot) went from 0.040 to 0.003 of the body level.
4. In the two largest classes the far segment does not turn with the near segment. Class 130 (13.5k particles): covariance ratio 0.09, CI -0.07 to 0.24. Class 31: difference -7.3 deg², CI -12 to -2.

Two qualifications on "genuinely shorter". First, it is a 2D projected length: out-of-plane tilt of the attached DNA would also shorten it. Linear density argues weakly against tilt (it is lower for dot classes, 5.7 versus 7.6, whereas tilt would raise it), but this is not decisive. Second, free rods themselves are only about 109 Å, not the 170 Å of a straight 50 bp duplex, so "full length" here means about 109 Å in projection.
measure.numbers:
Setup and checks
- Class groups (classes with ≥500 particles): 15 dot-at-end classes with 82,768 particles, and 16 free (dot-free) rod classes with 12,662 particles.
- Pose convention re-verified on 3,000 A1 particles: rot-th_shift-_particleframe, r = 0.211 (next best 0.029), the same as script 17. Particle contrast sign is -1.
- My plain re-averages correlate 0.85-0.89 with the CryoSPARC class averages, so the class-frame mapping is correct.
- 82,382 particles were read from 7,925 files. Slurm job 60648377 took about 6 minutes.

(a) Hinge-insensitive lengths from the class averages
- Dot classes: DNA length = mass-profile end minus 17 Å.
  - Particle-weighted median 75.4 Å (95% CI 72.3-87.4); mean 77.4 Å (69.2-84.5).
  - Largest classes: 123 = 75 Å, 130 = 87 Å, 31 = 76 Å.
  - Long minority: 13 = 102 Å, 52 = 96 Å, 97 = 109 Å.
- Free rods, end to end: median 108.7 Å (103.1-113.1); mean 108.6 Å.
- Gap (free minus dot):
  - Median 33.3 Å (19.4-38.6); mean 31.2 Å (22.4-40.7).
  - If the DNA starts at the dot centre (0 Å offset instead of 17 Å): 16.3 Å (2.2-21.5).
  - Using only the 10 named dot classes: 33.3 Å (18.8-39.6).
  - Using half-max lengths: 39.3 Å (24.3-45.1).
- 11.5% of dot-class particles are at free length (within 15 Å).
- Both groups are far below the 170 Å of a straight 50 bp duplex.

(a) End sharpness and widening
- End sigma: dot median 15.3 Å (12.0-18.5); free median 9.0 Å (7.9-10.5).
- End sigma divided by each average's point-spread sigma: dot 2.18, free 2.08. The ratio of the two is 1.05.
- Width-implied angle: dot median 5.8° (3.2-8.1); free 3.8° (3.2-4.8).
- Forward-blur calibration (largest free averages pivoted about a point 17 Å beyond one end):
  - Half-max under-read: 0 / -2.7 / -5.5 / -7.4 / -13.7 / -18.8 / -24.0 Å at 0 / 4 / 8 / 12 / 16 / 20 / 25°.
  - Mass-profile end changes by at most +1.1 Å; end sigma goes from 6.3 to 8.0 Å.
- Predicted half-max under-read: -4.0 Å at the dot median angle, -7.0 Å at the largest dot-class angle (11.2°, class 123).

(b) Re-alignment (all 66,563 particles of the 10 named classes; reference covers 30-80 Å from the dot)
- Mass-profile end change, particle-weighted: -1.21 Å. Half-max change: -8.9 Å, because noisy angles blur the rod.
- Far-zone (100-170 Å) mass relative to body: 0.040 before, 0.003 after.
- Noise-free hinge spread, sqrt(cov(S1,S2)): weighted 3.21° (0-5.7). Per-particle angle SD is 5-16°, so single-particle angles are mostly noise.
- Near-segment angles correlate (p < 0.01) in 6 of 10 classes.
- Near-to-far correlation is positive (p < 0.01) only in class 123 (r = 0.024).
- Covariance ratio, far versus near (1 = rigid rod continues out to 100-170 Å; 0 = nothing there):
  - 123: 0.31 (0.09-0.54)
  - 130: 0.09 (-0.07-0.24)
  - 31: difference -7.3 deg² (-12.1 to -2.1)
  - Other classes have CIs that include both 0 and 1.
- Positive controls 97 and 87: ratio -0.02 and -0.56, with CIs spanning 0 and 1, so the test is underpowered (see caveats).

(c) Helical repeat
- No class in either group has a 30-38 Å periodogram peak with SNR ≥ 3.
- Median SNR at 34 Å: dot 2.6, free 1.06. Repeats cannot be counted in these 12 Å averages.

(d) Linear density (my re-averages)
- Dot 5.71 versus free 7.64 (per-particle-sigma·Å). Tilt-foreshortening would raise the dot value; it is lower.
caveats: The pre-set decision rule returned 'mixed/inconclusive', not H1. One H1 condition failed: class 123 shows a small positive near-to-far angle correlation. My reading is that this reflects a small long-DNA minority, but the outcome is the rule's, and I have not changed the rule after seeing it.

The size of the gap depends on where the DNA starts relative to the dot centre. With a 17 Å offset the gap is 33 Å (19-39); if the DNA end projects over the sfGFP (0 Å) it is 16 Å (2-21). The sign is robust but the magnitude (about 5-10 bp) is not.

The 2D projected length cannot separate a genuinely shorter duplex from an out-of-plane tilted one. The lower dot-class linear density argues against tilt, but partial occupancy within classes could also lower it.
Free rods are about 109 Å, not 170 Å, so even free duplex is short in projection (fraying, tilt, or rods that are not all 50 bp). 'Full length' therefore means 'free-rod length' here.

The far-segment angle test is underpowered. The positive controls 97 and 87 have visible DNA reaching only about 0-20 Å into the far segment (100-170 Å), and they did not reach significance. Per-particle angle SNR is low (near-segment correlations of only 0.04-0.11), so the strong negative results rest on the two largest classes (123 and 130) and on 31.

Re-alignment cannot sharpen anything at this SNR: per-particle angle noise (5-16° SD) exceeds the true spread (about 3°). The half-max length therefore drops after re-alignment. A first trial with a 30-100 Å reference snapped the half-max to the reference end (reference bias), so I shortened the reference to 30-80 Å and only interpret mass beyond 100 Å.

I changed several definitions after one trial run; each is documented with its justification in the script docstring. Dot/rod ratio cutoffs became 1.6 for dot classes and <1.3 for free rods (originally 2.3 and 2.0; my ratio is defined differently from the first-pass column). The width cap for dot classes is 25 Å, because a 15 Å cap would have excluded the wide class 130, which is the hinge signature under test. I added a 'dot within 100 Å of box centre' rule and a separate-blob gap test, which exclude ice class 58 and the dot-gap-dot class 53. I used all particles of each class rather than 3-5k subsets, and added classes 97 and 87 as long-DNA positive controls.

My half-max lengths are about 20-40 Å shorter than the first-pass A1_class_lengths.csv values (for example, class 133: 129.5 Å versus 152.6 Å), so that column over-reads relative to these measures. The overlays in figure panel (a) confirm my end positions sit at the visible rod ends.

The lone-dot-plus-haze classes 105 and 12 (37% of particles) are excluded. Their DNA (if any) is unmeasured and could include strongly misaligned or long rods. Class 147's erf end fit is unstable (end sigma 38 Å, continuous fade).
The helical-repeat measurement (c) failed: there is no 34 Å peak in any 12 Å average, so it gives no independent duplex-length count.
No git commit was made, per the task. Intermediate files are on netscratch, which is purged.

problems: Only part of the verdict survives. The CryoSPARC class-average mass profiles do show most DOT classes falling to background by r = 110-126 Å from the dot, which is where free-length DNA (about 109 + 17 Å) would still be at body level. Examples of mass/body at r = 110-126 Å: class 123 0.24, 130 0.04, 31 0.04, 103 -0.02, 114 0.01. Rotation about the dot within ±30° cannot move the sector-integrated end, so an in-plane hinge cannot produce this gap. That much holds. Several supporting claims and numbers do not.

Evidence item 3 (re-alignment) is circular for L_end. The script itself defines the ±30° sector mass as invariant to rotation about the dot, so a dL_end of -1.2 Å is guaranteed by construction and is not independent evidence. Worse, the re-averages behind item 3 are phase-flipped only with a 15 Å low-pass, and their mass profiles are dominated by fringes. The profiles are non-monotonic: class 123 is 1.09/0.31/0.82/1.24 at r = 40/48/56/64 Å, and class 130 is -7.7 times body at r = 40 Å. The erf fits on them give sig_end of about 1.6-3 Å, which is physically impossible after a 15 Å low-pass. So dL_end, the far-zone fractions and the re-average lengths (5-12 Å shorter than the CryoSPARC averages for both groups) are unreliable.

The 'far-zone mass 0.040 to 0.003' figure is a particle-weighted mean of per-class values from -0.16 to +0.23 (the noise floor from negative halos is about ±0.15). The drop comes mostly from class 130, whose ill-defined body median makes its value go from 0.085 to -0.079. Class 123, the largest dot class, has a far-zone fraction of 0.23 before and 0.22 after re-alignment. That is the same as the long-DNA class 13 (0.23), not 'nothing there'.

Evidence item 4 (far-segment covariance) uses the wrong null. 'Ratio = 1 for a rigid rod' holds only for a linear, unbiased angle estimator. Here the angle is an argmax over a bounded ±30° grid, so when signal is weak the estimate is partly random. The expected ratio then scales with the S3 lock-on fraction times prox/(S1·S2) lock-on, and is well below 1 even if the rod is there. Also, S3 = 100-170 Å overlaps a free-length attached duplex (ending near r ≈ 126 Å) by only about 26 Å, because the design assumed a 170 Å rod. The positive controls 97 and 87 fail (-0.02 and -0.56), which confirms this. Class 130's CI excluding 1 therefore does not argue against full-length DNA. Item 4 should be dropped as evidence either way, and the class-123 'S3-positive' flag that tripped the decision rule is equally uninformative.

The linear-density tilt argument (5.71 vs 7.64) is invalid. Free classes, all carrying the same DNA, range from 2.57 to 21.05, an 8-fold spread, and the value anti-correlates with class size (Spearman -0.66, p = 0.006). It is a median of raw, fringe-dominated phase-flipped profiles with no background subtraction, and the DOT mean is pulled down by class 130 (1.47). A better internal standard (CryoSPARC-average rod mass per Å divided by dot mass) gives about 15-19 for both the short mid-size dot classes (103, 145, 138, 114, 54, 92, 146; DNA 69-80 Å) and the long ones (87, 52, 13, 97; 90-109 Å). Uniform tilt foreshortening to 75/109 would predict about 1.45 times higher for the short classes, so this weakly argues against tilt for those classes. Classes 123 and 130, however, have a rod only 1/3 to 1/5 as strong relative to the dot (5.2 and 3.1), which suggests partial rod occupancy or smear. Their lengths therefore describe only a subset of their particles.

The calibration is misquoted. The JSON mean half-max under-read at 25° is -19.5 Å, not -24.0 Å. Per class it is erratic: classes 111 and 110 saturate at -5.6 to -7.0 Å, while 133 and 30 jump about 20 Å between 12° and 16-20°, reaching -28 to -36 Å (a threshold artefact of the half-max). So '>25° needed for the 33 Å gap' is not robust for half-max: for 2 of 4 calibration rods, 16-20° already gives at least 28 Å of under-read. This is moot for L_end, which is insensitive to an in-plane hinge by construction, and comparing the L_end gap with the half-max calibration curve mixes two different measures.

Several counts are wrong. The 15 DOT classes hold 76,607 particles, not 82,768, and the 16 FREE classes hold 11,995, not 12,662. The 82,382 particles read are DOT10 (66,563) + 97 + 87 + FREE. A1 has 223,536 particles. The 'long minority' fraction of 0.115 comes from classes 13, 52 and 97 only; class 87 (DNA 90 Å) falls below the 93.7 Å cutoff, even though the verdict names it.

'About 88% of dot-at-end particles are shorter' overstates the result. It is a class-level label applied to 76,607 particles (34% of A1). Within-class heterogeneity is visible: DOT ends are 70% broader in raw terms than FREE ends (sig_end 15.3 vs 9.0 Å). The PSF-scaled ratio of 1.05 hides this because the 'PSF' is inferred from body width that already includes the smear; class 130's PSF is 18.4 Å. I fitted two components to the CryoSPARC mass profiles: a short component plus a fixed free-length step at 125.7 Å with sigma 9 Å. Estimated full-length fractions: 0.12-0.32 for class 123, 0-0.27 for 130, 0.09-0.16 for 31, 92, 145 and 114, and 0.45-0.55 for 52 and 13. The particle-weighted fraction is about 0.19 with a 160 Å fit range and is sensitive to the fit range. So the full-length minority is roughly 10-25%, not 12%.

Class 147's erf fit is degenerate (L_end 63 Å is less than L_ridge 81 Å; sig_end 38 Å) but enters at 46 Å with weight 6,851. This biases the mean down. The median is robust (75.4 vs 75.9 Å without it).

'Hinge blur does not explain' applies only to an in-plane hinge. The in-plane hinge is already absorbed by 2D alignment, and the mass end is invariant to it by design. An out-of-plane hinge, which foreshortens the projection, is the real H2/H3 alternative. It is constrained only by the internal-standard check above, and only for the mid-size classes.

There is a selection bias toward short, rigid DNA. Classes 105 and 12 (lone dot plus haze, 37%) and 20 other excluded classes (about 30k particles, several with 50-80% dot labels and rods reaching 77-106 Å from the dot, e.g. 2, 20, 16, 131) are unmeasured. Flexible or long attached duplexes would preferentially fail to average and land in exactly these classes.

Methods that checked out: the pose convention (rot-th_shift-_particleframe, r = 0.211 vs 0.029, the same as script 17); the re-alignment rotation sign (rod_refs and the resampling rotation are consistent); the class-resampling bootstrap; and the sign of the gap across junction offsets (offset 0: 16 Å, CI 2-21; offset 17 Å: 33 Å, CI 19-39).
skeptics.corrected_statement:
For the 15 measurable dot-at-end classes (76,607 particles, 34% of A1), I used the CryoSPARC class-average radial mass profiles (density integrated over a ±30° sector about the dot). The duplex visible on sfGFP ends at a median of about 75 Å past the sfGFP surface (92 Å from the dot centre). That is 16-33 Å short of the free-rod length of about 109 Å: 33 Å (CI 19-39) with a 17 Å junction offset, 16 Å (CI 2-21) with 0 Å. The free rods are themselves only about 109 Å in projection, not the 170 Å of a straight 50 bp duplex.

An in-plane hinge at the attachment cannot cause this gap, because rotation about the dot does not move the sector-integrated end. A real free-rod average pivoted by up to 25° shifts it by about 1 Å.

The re-alignment result and the far-segment angle-covariance test are not independent evidence and should be dropped. Re-alignment is circular for this measure, and its phase-flipped re-averages are dominated by fringes. The covariance test's null of ratio = 1 is wrong for a weak-signal argmax estimator, its window mostly lies beyond free-length DNA, and both positive controls fail. The linear-density argument against tilt is also invalid: free classes vary 8-fold.

A dot-mass-normalised rod density from the CryoSPARC averages is similar for short and long dot classes. That weakly argues against out-of-plane tilt for the mid-size short classes. It does not cover the two largest classes (123 and 130), whose rods are 3-5 times weaker relative to the dot.

The classes are not homogeneous. Two-component fits suggest about 10-25% of dot-class particles carry free-length DNA: whole classes 13, 52 and 97, plus subsets inside 123, 130, 31 and others. So the short population is roughly 75-90% of the measured dot-class particles, not a firm 88%.

Conclusion: within the classes that average, the data favour H1 (a shorter attached duplex) over H2/H3 with an in-plane hinge. An out-of-plane hinge, causing foreshortening, is only weakly excluded. The 63% of particles in the haze or excluded classes, which is where flexible full-length adducts would most likely end up, are unmeasured. The pre-set decision rule's 'mixed/inconclusive' outcome is the honest label. Corrected figures: at 25° the calibrated half-max under-read is 19.5 Å (mean, range 5.6-35.9 Å), not 24 Å; the class groups hold 76,607 dot-class and 11,995 free-class particles.

problems: Narrow claim holds: in-plane hinge blur does not explain the short half-max length. The calibration (mass-profile end moves <=1.1 A at 25 deg while half-max under-reads 7-30 A) and the small width-implied spread (dot 5.8 deg vs free 3.8 deg) are sound. The broader claim, that the duplex on sfGFP is genuinely shorter and that this favours H1, goes further than the data.

Out-of-plane tilt (foreshortening) is the same physical hinge seen along the beam, and it is not excluded. The linear-density argument against it fails. (i) Unweighted class medians are identical: DOT 7.43 vs FREE 7.35. The weighted 5.71 vs 7.64 comes from class 130 (1.47, a barely visible rod; L_end error 6.6 A) and class 123. (ii) Across the 16 FREE classes, linear density is strongly anti-correlated with rod length (Spearman -0.74, p=0.001) and with class size (-0.66, p=0.006). So density is confounded by class size: the large DOT classes would read low regardless. The length correlation also suggests foreshortened, denser views are present among the free rods themselves. A sfGFP adsorbed at the air-water interface with its DNA tilted into the ice would give exactly a short end that fades gradually.

End sharpness does not cleanly pass. Raw end sigma is 15.3 A for dot classes vs 9.0 A for free (difference CI -9.4 to -2.8, excludes 0). The PSF-scaled ratio of 1.05 uses body width as the PSF, and body width is itself inflated in dot classes (class 130: 19 A). On plain re-averages, end-sigma fits fall to 1.2-3 A, below the PSF, so the erf fits depend on which pipeline made the average.

The size and pass/fail of the gap depend on the 17 A junction offset. With a 0 A offset the gap is 16.3 A (CI 2.2-21.5). That falls inside the pre-registered H2/H3 clause ('within 20 A of FREE'). DNA that crosses over sfGFP in projection could hide more length; an invisible BCN-TEG linker would push the other way. The CI of the 33 A gap (19.4-38.6) also does not exclude values below the 25 A H1 threshold.

The '88% shorter / 11.5% at free length' split is class-level and depends on the pipeline. On the script's own plain re-averages, class 130 reads 96 A DNA (free 103.6 A re-averaged), so 31.7% of dot-class particles fall within 15 A of free length (classes 130, 13, 52, 97). Within-class mass tails in the CryoSPARC averages imply that roughly 13-30% of dot-class particles have projected DNA of at least 94-105 A. The largest class, 123, has mass extending to ~130 A from the dot, far-zone mass 0.23 in the re-average, and the positive S3 correlation. The long minority is therefore about 15-35%, not about 12%.

Re-alignment evidence (point 3) is not informative. The weighted far-zone change from 0.040 to 0.003 is mostly baseline noise: class 130 goes from +0.085 to -0.079, and several classes sit at -0.10 to -0.17. The report itself concedes that angle noise (5-16 deg) exceeds the true spread (about 3 deg). Point 4 is underpowered, since the positive controls 97 and 87 fail.

Scope and selection bias. The DOT group holds only about 50% of round-1 dot_long_rod particles; about 46% (56k) are in excluded classes, mostly the haze classes 105 and 12. That is where strongly hinged or tilted full-length adducts would end up. The FREE reference contains only about 10% of rod_no_dot particles, chosen by width <=15 A, length >=80 A and a clean-rod criterion. So the conclusion covers dot classes whose rod averages, not 'dot-at-end particles' in general.

Neither population is a full 50 bp duplex: free rods are about 109 A (and the W3 3D map of 'rod, no dot' particles is a ~110 A rod with a lobe at one end, so free rods may themselves be adducts), and dot DNA is about 75-92 A, against 170 A expected. H2/H3 as stated predicts a full-length duplex, and that is absent for both groups. The test therefore compares attached DNA with the free-rod population; it does not test complete vs incomplete duplex.
The pre-registered rule returned 'mixed/inconclusive'. Reporting the result as favouring H1 for 88% of particles overstates what the rule found.
skeptics.corrected_statement:
In-plane hinge blur is ruled out as the cause of the short half-max lengths of the dot-at-end classes. A pure in-plane rotation about the dot leaves the radial mass-profile end unchanged: in calibration, 25 deg moves it by at most +1.1 A. The measured in-plane spread is small: about 6 deg from class-average widening, and about 3 deg noise-free per particle. On the hinge-insensitive measure, the DNA visible in the dot classes whose rod averages (about 83k particles, 37% of A1) projects to a median of about 75 A from the sfGFP surface (17 A offset). Free rods project to about 109 A. The gap is about 33 A (CI 19-39), but only about 16 A (2-21) if the DNA starts at the dot centre. Its sign is robust; its size, roughly 5-10 bp, is not.

This does NOT establish a genuinely shorter duplex (H1) over a flexibly attached duplex of free-rod length:
- Out-of-plane tilt of the attached DNA is not excluded. The linear-density argument against tilt is confounded by class size: unweighted class medians are equal (7.4 vs 7.4), and free-rod density falls with free-rod length (rho = -0.74).
- Dot ends are blunter than free ends in raw terms (15 vs 9 A), which fits either a spread of lengths or a spread of tilts.

The long minority is larger than reported. By class-average tails and plain re-averages, about 15-35% of dot-class particles carry projected DNA at or near free-rod length. This includes part of the largest class, 123: its mass reaches about 130 A from the dot and its far-segment angle correlation is positive.

Scope:
- The about 56k round-1 dot_long_rod particles in excluded classes (mostly the lone-dot-plus-haze classes 105/12) are unmeasured, and they are where strongly hinged or tilted adducts would land.
- Neither population approaches the 170 A of a straight 50 bp duplex. The W3 3D map of free rods is about 110 A with a terminal lobe, so 'full length' here means only 'free-rod length'.

The pre-registered rule outcome, mixed/inconclusive, stands. The data weakly favour 'attached DNA usually projects shorter than free DNA', but they cannot tell an incomplete or yielded duplex (H1) from a tilted mono-adduct (H2/H3) without tilt-pair data or 3D of the dot classes.
